title: Zephyrine and the Current
premise: Paloma Montrose has spent seven years outrunning a manslaughter charge by flying cargo into the interior, where the river keeps its secrets. When a flood recedes and exposes a chest bearing the seal of San Marisol—a nation erased from maps forty years ago—Paloma and their passenger, archivist Ines Vidal, realize the chest holds proof that the concession company's land claims were built on forged treaties. With permits expiring in three weeks and the company's enforcers closing in, Paloma must fly the evidence out through weather, betrayal, and their own past, choosing at last between permanent flight and standing still to face justice on their own terms. The expedition gets home; Paloma surrenders to the authorities carrying the chest, betting that truth outweighs the charge—and wins a trial instead of a cell.
about_author: Freya Okafor is a former bush-strip radio operator who spent a decade in remote river settlements before turning to fiction. She writes about people who live where the law thins out and conscience has to do the work.

chapters.title: Fuel, Rumors, Rain
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. A routine medicine run into the interior establishes Paloma's rules: no names, no stops longer than an hour, no questions answered. A settler mentions the river dropped two meters overnight after the flood. Emotional beat: competent loneliness—Paloma is good at this life and knows exactly what it costs.

chapters.title: The Passenger with Two Suitcases
chapters.summary: Ines Vidal hires Paloma for a survey flight, paying too much and explaining too little. Paloma takes the money anyway because the plane needs an engine overhaul. POV alternates: Ines watches Paloma's hands; Paloma watches Ines's suitcases. Emotional beat: wary mutual sizing-up between two people both hiding something.

chapters.title: What the River Gave Back
chapters.summary: On a low pass over a collapsed bank, Paloma spots metal glinting in the mud. They land against their own better judgment. The chest bears the seal of San Marisol, a country that officially never existed. Ines goes white. Emotional beat: awe curdling instantly into fear—the moment staying invisible stops being possible.

chapters.title: A Nation That Isn't on the Map
chapters.summary: Ines reveals she's an archivist whose grandmother was San Marisolan; the chest likely holds treaty documents proving the concession company's land grants were forgeries. Paloma wants to leave it. Ines argues they've already been seen by a company patrol boat. Emotional beat: reluctant partnership sealed by shared danger rather than trust.

chapters.title: The Weight of Paper
chapters.summary: They open the chest at a derelict mission station: treaties signed under duress, a census of disappeared villages, photographs. Paloma recognizes a village name from their own past—the settlement where their accident happened. Emotional beat: the documents stop being abstract and become personal.

chapters.title: Company Men
chapters.summary: Two men from Meridian Concessions arrive at the mission asking about 'salvage rights.' Paloma lies smoothly; Ines nearly breaks. Afterward, Paloma realizes the patrol boat photographed their plane. Emotional beat: the hunter's chill—Paloma knows how professionals work because they used to be one.

chapters.title: Seven Years of Nowhere
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, Paloma's POV. The night of the accident: a charter overloaded to pay off debts, a passenger dead, a falsified logbook, and a choice to run rather than stand trial. Emotional beat: shame examined honestly for the first time; we learn why stopping costs more.

chapters.title: The Permit Clock
chapters.summary: Ines decodes the documents' significance: if the original San Marisol treaties surface before the concession permits expire in nineteen days, the land claims collapse in court. Meridian will do anything to prevent that. Emotional beat: hope with a deadline—suddenly there's a reason to move toward trouble instead of away.

chapters.title: Old Friends, New Prices
chapters.summary: Paloma seeks fuel and help from Toma, a river trader who owes them. Toma agrees—but warns that Meridian has posted a reward for information about a blue-and-white bush plane. Someone has already sold them out once. Emotional beat: the economy of loyalty in places without law.

chapters.title: Detour Through the Smoke
chapters.summary: Flying the chest south, they must thread through burn-off smoke to avoid a Meridian checkpoint airstrip. An engine coughs; Paloma lands on a sandbar as dusk falls. Ines confesses she tipped off one person about the find—her brother, who works for Meridian's legal office. Emotional beat: betrayal that isn't quite betrayal.

chapters.title: Sandbar Night
chapters.summary: Stranded overnight, the two trade truths. Ines explains her family's erasure from official records; Paloma admits the manslaughter charge aloud for the first time in seven years. Emotional beat: intimacy earned through confession—the chest has made honesty cheaper than lies.

chapters.title: The Brother's Offer
chapters.summary: Ines's brother Mateo finds them via the sandbar's radio chatter. He offers Meridian's terms: hand over the chest, get immunity, Ines's family name restored on the company's terms. Ines refuses; Mateo warns them the enforcement team leaves at dawn. Emotional beat: grief for family weaponized against you.

chapters.title: Dawn Departure
chapters.summary: Paloma repairs the engine by headlamp while Ines hides the most damning documents in her clothing as insurance. They lift off minutes before the enforcement floatplane arrives, bullets cracking past the tail. Emotional beat: terror transmuted into fierce clarity—there is no going back now.

chapters.title: Grounded
chapters.summary: Storm forces them down at a mission clinic where Paloma once delivered medicine. The nuns shelter them but word travels fast; Meridian offers the mission funding in exchange for the fugitives. The Mother Superior chooses the documents over the donation. Emotional beat: unexpected solidarity from strangers who remember kindness.

chapters.title: The Copy Problem
chapters.summary: Ines insists on making duplicates before any final move—one set to a journalist, one hidden. Paloma argues copies mean more people at risk; Ines argues a single chest can simply disappear. They fight bitterly, then compromise. Emotional beat: the ethics of evidence—what survival justifies.

chapters.title: Toma's Price
chapters.summary: Toma agrees to smuggle them to the capital by river barge—for payment Paloma never expected: Paloma's plane, and the truth of what happened seven years ago, told to him directly. Emotional beat: the price of survival made literal; Paloma pays it.

chapters.title: Downriver
chapters.summary: Three days on the barge among cargo and suspicion. Meridian agents board at a lock, checking papers. Ines bluffs with flawless bureaucratic confidence; Paloma, disguised as deckhand, nearly gives them away when recognized by a former client. Emotional beat: sustained dread broken by absurd, human luck.

chapters.title: Capital of Forgetting
chapters.summary: The capital: ministries, expired stamps, officials who don't want the past reopened. Ines petitions a judge known for integrity; he warns that without someone willing to testify publicly, the documents are hearsay. All eyes turn to Paloma. Emotional beat: the trap of the only honest option.

chapters.title: What Stopping Costs
chapters.summary: Meridian's fixer corners Paloma with a final offer: exile, money, the charge quietly buried—if the chest vanishes. Paloma walks the city all night weighing seven years of running against one act of standing still. Emotional beat: the decision crystallizes; running was always the more expensive choice.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Climax. At the permit hearing, Paloma surrenders to the court, confesses the falsified logbook and the flight, and enters the San Marisol documents into evidence, testifying to everything. Meridian's lawyers implode as the forged treaties unravel. Emotional beat: catharsis through self-indictment—justice claimed from inside the law at last.

chapters.title: Sentencing
chapters.summary: Resolution begins. Paloma receives a reduced sentence—community service and license suspension—because the confession and evidence weighed heavily. Ines's family records are restored; the concessions voided. Mateo resigns from Meridian and brings internal memos. Emotional beat: justice imperfect but real; the price paid turns out to be bearable.

chapters.title: The Current Again
chapters.summary: Epilogue, one year later. Paloma, licensed again, flies Ines and repatriated San Marisol archives back upriver to a restored village. The chest returns home. Paloma stops at the old mission without hurrying. Emotional beat: arrival—movement chosen freely at last, the current no longer something to flee but to ride.
